user_message: How does the village make decisions, and what is the job of the Keeper of the Banyan?
assistant_response:
**Decision-Making Process in Mangala**

- **Community Meetings**: Decisions are made collectively under the Talking Tree, where villagers sit in a circle and discuss issues.
- **Inclusive Participation**: Anyone, including the youngest child, may speak by holding a smooth river stone, ensuring that all voices are heard.

**Role of the Keeper of the Banyan**

- **Facilitator**: The Keeper of the Banyan ensures that everyone is heard and helps the circle reach fair decisions.
- **Non-Authoritative**: The Keeper does not give orders but facilitates discussion and consensus-building.

The Village of Mangala
 A Story of People, a River and a Hidden Spring
 A made-up story, written in simple words. There is nothing to calculate here.

This guide tells the story of one imaginary village. Read it slowly. Every chapter has a
few simple ideas, and the story builds from one chapter to the next.


--- Page 3 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 3
1. Welcome to Mangala
Mangala is a small village that sits at the bottom of a tall hill called Blue Hill. A river
called the Silver River runs past the village on its way to the sea. In the morning,
when the sun hits the water, the whole river shines like a ribbon of silver. That is how
it got its name.
The houses of Mangala are made of mud and wood, and most of them have red clay
roofs. Between the houses there are narrow lanes, small gardens and a great many
chickens. Everyone in the village knows everyone else. If a child falls and scrapes a
knee, three neighbours will arrive with water and a cloth before the parents have even
heard the noise.
Mangala is not rich. There is no big market, no factory and no tall building. But the
people say that they have the three things that matter most: clean water, good
neighbours and a place to tell stories in the evening.
Why this story matters
This is the story of how Mangala nearly lost its river, and how a curious young girl
helped save it. Along the way you will meet the villagers, learn about their food and
festivals, and see how a village can look after the land that looks after it.


--- Page 4 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 4
2. How the village began
Long ago, there was no village here, only forest and a wide, slow river. A boatman
named Devraj was carrying a load of rice to a town far down the coast. One evening
his boat got stuck in the soft mud near a bend in the river. He could not push it free, so
he decided to wait for the morning.
During the night it rained heavily, and when Devraj woke up the river had risen and
lifted his boat. But he did not leave. He looked at the green hill, the clear water, the
fish jumping and the good red earth along the bank, and he thought: "This is a place
where people could live well."
Devraj went back up the river and told his family and friends about what he had seen.
Some did not believe him, but a few came to look. They liked what they found. They
built the first houses near the bend where his boat had been stuck, and they named the
place Mangala, a word that means "good fortune".
The first banyan seed
On the first day in the new village, Devraj planted a banyan seed in the middle of the
clearing. He said that a village without a shady tree is like a house without a roof.
Over many years the seed grew into an enormous tree, and it is still there today.


--- Page 5 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 5
3. The people of Mangala
Mangala has many families, but a few people are known to everyone. You will meet
them again and again in this story.

What they are known for

everything that ever happened

Knowing which herbs and leaves help

than anyone

Asking questions, and finding things

Tara lives with her grandmother near the edge of the village. She is always asking
"why?" Sometimes this makes the grown-ups tired, but Amma Saraswati says that a
child who asks "why" is a child who will one day solve a problem.


--- Page 6 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 6
4. The Talking Tree
In the middle of Mangala stands the old banyan tree planted by Devraj. Its branches
spread so wide that the shade covers the whole village square, and its hanging roots
have grown into thick pillars. Children call it the Talking Tree, because so many
conversations happen beneath it.
Whenever something important must be decided, the villagers meet under the Talking
Tree. They sit on the ground in a big circle. Anyone may speak, even the youngest
child, but only one person talks at a time. The speaker holds a smooth river stone, and
when they have finished they pass it to the next person.
The Keeper of the Banyan
The village has no king and no boss. Instead, the circle chooses a Keeper of the
Banyan, a person trusted by everyone. The Keeper does not give orders. Their job is
to make sure that everybody is heard and that the circle reaches a decision that is fair.
The present Keeper is Meenakshi, who was chosen because she is known for listening
before she speaks.
There is a saying in Mangala: "Two ears and one mouth, that is how the Keeper
works."


--- Page 7 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 7
5. A day in Mangala
Life in the village follows the sun. Before it is light, the roosters begin to crow, and
the first smoke rises from the kitchens. By the time the sky turns pink, Gopal is
already on the river in his small wooden boat, casting his net.
In the morning the children walk to the school under the neem tree, carrying slates
and small bags of lunch. The women fetch water from the village wells and talk as
they walk. Ravi lights his kiln and begins to shape clay on his wheel. Hema goes to
the edge of the forest to collect leaves and roots for her medicines.
At midday the heat becomes strong and everybody rests. Some people sleep in the
shade of the Talking Tree, others sit on their porches and mend baskets or tools. The
only sounds are the buzzing of insects and the distant splash of a fish.
In the late afternoon the village wakes up again. Children run to the river to swim and
play. Ibrahim checks his beehives. Gopal returns with his catch and shares some with
neighbours who have no fish. As the sun goes down, lamps are lit and the smell of
dinner floats through the lanes.
Evening stories
After dinner, people gather under the Talking Tree. Amma Saraswati sits on a low
stool, and the children settle around her feet. She tells stories of clever animals, brave
travellers and the old days of the village. Nobody is in a hurry to go to bed.


--- Page 8 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 8
6. Food and kitchens
The food of Mangala is simple but tasty, and almost everything comes from nearby
fields, the river or the forest. Each kitchen has a clay stove, and each family has a
favourite way of cooking.
What people eat
  Millet porridge is eaten for breakfast, usually with a little salt and buttermilk.
 Rice and lentils are the main meal at midday, often with vegetables from the
garden.
 Fresh river fish, fried with spices, is a favourite dish on days when Gopal's
catch is good.
 Mango pickle is made every summer and stored in clay jars; every family
guards its own recipe.
 Jaggery sweets, made from raw sugar, are given to guests and to children who
have done well at school.
Visitors are always offered food. In Mangala, it is considered rude to let a guest leave
without at least a cup of tea and a small sweet. Even a stranger who is just passing
through will be invited to sit and eat.
Sharing
When a family has more than it needs, it shares. If someone's harvest is poor,
neighbours bring food. If someone is ill, the others cook for them. This habit of
sharing is the reason nobody in Mangala has ever gone hungry for long.


--- Page 9 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 9
7. Blue pots and golden honey
Two things made in Mangala are known far beyond the village: Ravi's blue pots and
Ibrahim's honey.
The blue pots
Ravi digs fine clay from the riverbank, cleans it, and shapes it on a spinning wheel.
When the pot is dry, he paints it with a special glaze made from crushed blue stones
that he collects from the slopes of Blue Hill. After firing in the kiln, the glaze turns a
deep, shining blue, the colour of the sky just after sunset. Traders come from distant
towns to buy these pots, and the money helps the village buy salt, cloth and tools.
The golden honey
Ibrahim keeps his hives at the edge of the forest, where wild flowers grow. He says
that the bees are his teachers. "They never rush, and they never waste," he tells the
children. His honey is thick and golden, with a faint taste of flowers. He never takes
all of it; he always leaves enough for the bees to eat through the cold season.
Ravi and Ibrahim are good friends. Ravi makes the jars that hold Ibrahim's honey, and
Ibrahim gives Ravi honey for his tea. It is the sort of arrangement that keeps a village
working well.


--- Page 10 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 10
8. School and stories
The school of Mangala has no walls on two sides. It is a simple roof held up by
wooden posts, built under a large neem tree. When it rains, the children move to the
old grain store. Nisha, the teacher, says that learning does not need a grand building;
it needs only curiosity and a few good books.
The children learn reading, writing and arithmetic, but they also learn things that no
book can teach. They learn to name the birds and plants. They learn how to read the
weather from the clouds. They learn the old songs of the village. And once a week
they walk to the river to see how it is doing.
The river lesson
Every week Nisha takes the class to the riverbank. They look at the water, the plants
and the animals. They notice if the river is clear or muddy, high or low, and they write
what they see in a big notebook called the River Book. This habit, started by Nisha
many years ago, will turn out to be very important later in the story.
Amma Saraswati often visits the school to tell stories. Her favourite is the tale of
Devraj and the stuck boat, and the children ask for it again and again.


--- Page 11 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 11
9. Lantern Night
The biggest festival of the year is Lantern Night. It takes place after the rains have
ended, when the river is full and the air smells fresh. The festival is a way of saying
thank you to the Silver River for all that it gives.
For days before the festival, the children make paper lanterns. They fold thin coloured
paper over small wooden frames and place a tiny oil lamp inside each one. Everyone
makes a lantern, even the grown-ups, and each person makes a silent wish or a
thank-you as they work.
On the night of the festival, the whole village walks in a slow line to the riverbank. It
is quiet except for the soft sound of feet. Amma Saraswati speaks a few words of
thanks to the river. Then, one by one, people place their lanterns on the water. The
current takes them gently away, and the river fills with floating lights.
After the lanterns have floated out of sight, everyone returns to the village square.
There is music, dancing and a big shared meal. Ravi plays the drum, Hema sings, and
Gopal, who is a terrible dancer, is always dragged into the circle by the children.


--- Page 12 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 12
10. The year the river grew weak
One year, something went wrong. After the rains ended, the river did not look as full
as usual. By the time of Lantern Night the water was low and slow, and the lanterns
kept getting stuck on the sandbanks. The next season it was worse. Fish became
fewer, and Gopal came home with almost nothing in his net.
The wells began to run low. The women had to walk further to find clean water. The
clay Ravi needed was harder to dig, and Ibrahim's bees were restless because fewer
flowers were blooming. Everyone was worried, but no one knew the cause.
A meeting under the Talking Tree
Meenakshi called the villagers to the Talking Tree. They passed the stone from hand
to hand, and everyone gave a different idea. Some thought the weather was changing.
Others blamed bad luck. Gopal said that the river "felt tired", and Hema said that the
forest on the hill looked thinner than before.
Then Nisha stood up with the River Book. She read out her notes from the years
before. They showed that the river had been getting weaker slowly, year after year,
and that the trouble had started soon after a timber company from a faraway town had
cut many trees on the northern slopes of Blue Hill.
The villagers fell silent. They now understood that the weak river was not just bad
luck. But they still did not know exactly how the missing trees had hurt the river, or
what they could do about it.


--- Page 13 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 13
11. Tara and the hidden spring
After the meeting, young Tara could not stop thinking. She asked her grandmother,
"If the river comes from the hill, why would cutting trees matter?" Her grandmother
did not know, so Tara asked Amma Saraswati, who smiled and said, "Why don't you
go and look?"
The next morning Tara set out up Blue Hill with her friend Imran's little dog for
company. She followed the river's smaller streams upwards, looking for the place
where the water began. The slopes where the trees had been cut were bare and dusty.
Where the roots were gone, the soil was loose and rain had washed it into the streams.
High on the hill, Tara found an old path that she had never seen before. It led to a
mossy hollow where she heard a faint trickling sound. She pushed aside some bushes
and found a heap of fallen rocks. Water was seeping out between them, drop by drop,
instead of flowing freely.
The secret of the old spring
Tara ran back down the hill and told everyone what she had found. Amma Saraswati
gasped. "The Mother Spring!" she said. "My grandmother told me of it. It was the true
source of the Silver River, and I thought it was only a legend." Without the tree roots
to hold the soil, a landslide had tumbled rocks over the spring and nearly blocked it.
The next day the whole village climbed the hill. Gopal and Ravi lifted the big rocks,
Hema and Ibrahim carried the small ones, and the children cleared the mud with their
hands. By evening the water burst through, clear and cold, and ran down the hill in a
bright, loud stream.


--- Page 14 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 14
12. The Tree Promise
Within a few weeks, the Silver River had risen again. The fish returned, the wells
filled up, and the bees found flowers. Gopal's net was full once more.
But Meenakshi called the villagers to the Talking Tree one more time. "We have
cleared the spring," she said, "but the hill is still bare where the trees were cut. If we
do not heal it, the next heavy rains will wash the soil down again, and the spring will
be blocked once more."
So the villagers made a plan, which they called the Tree Promise. Each of its parts
was agreed by everyone in the circle:
 Every family will plant young trees on the bare slopes of Blue Hill, and look
after them until they are strong.
 No one will cut any tree on the hill without the agreement of the whole circle.
 The school children will visit the Mother Spring each season and record how it
looks in the River Book.
 The story of the spring will be told every year on Lantern Night, so that no child
ever forgets.
Tara was asked to plant the first tree, a small mango sapling, right beside the Mother
Spring. She dug the hole herself and patted the soil down around it. Amma Saraswati
said that this was the best moment she had seen in all her long life.


--- Page 15 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 15
13. Mangala today
Today the hillside above Mangala is green again. Young trees have grown tall, and
birds that had disappeared are singing in the branches. The Silver River is wide and
strong, and the lanterns on Lantern Night float far out before they vanish from sight.
Tara has grown up. She is now a teacher at the school under the neem tree, and she
takes her own class to the river every week to add to the River Book. The mango
sapling she planted is now a big tree, and its first fruits were shared with everyone in
the village.
What the story teaches
  Everything is connected. Trees on a hill can decide whether a river flows far
away.
 Careful observation matters. Nisha's River Book revealed the cause of the
problem when no one else could see it.
 Everyone's voice counts. A child found what the adults had missed, because the
circle was willing to listen to her.
 Communities can fix things together. The spring was cleared and the hill was
replanted because all the villagers took part.
 Stories keep wisdom alive. Because the old tale of the Mother Spring was
remembered, the spring could be found.
"A village is like a tree," Amma Saraswati likes to say. "What you see above the
ground is only half of it. The rest is roots, and the roots are the things we remember
and the promises we keep."


--- Page 16 ---
The Village of Mangala - Page 16
14. Word list
Word
Meaning

End of story.
